article.title: Hell Is Real
article.author: Eva Amar
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. In 2010, I was driving along Interstate 65 toward Bloomington, Indiana, when an enormous roadside billboard caught my attention. HELL IS REAL. I was returning to Indiana University, where my daughter had been raped four years earlier. Of all the messages I might have encountered along that highway, those three words seemed almost deliberately placed in my path. Back in the mid-1970s, when I worked as a systems support technician, my colleagues nicknamed me “Queen Irony.” If I said the sky was blue, it would almost immediately turn black and start pouring. The irony of that billboard was certainly not lost on me. I'd made that trip many times, returning for Take Back the Night rallies and other efforts to confront campus sexual violence. By then, I'd learned that my daughter's experience was hardly unique. In 2006, weeks before finishing her freshman year at Indiana University, my daughter called me, sobbing. She had been raped. Related: Charity Begins at Home What followed was an education I never wanted, membership in a club I never imagined joining, and a painful awakening to the failures of a system I had trusted to protect my daughter. I learned that the man she accused had a prior felony battery conviction and had been placed on a three-day psychiatric hold. There had been troubling incidents involving other young women. Yet he had been allowed to return to a coeducational residence hall. Evidence wasn't properly preserved. Prosecutors declined charges. The university carried on. My daughter survived. But what I learned about the institutions entrusted with protecting young women changed the direction of my life. A College Campus Is No Ivory Tower College is supposed to be a young woman's introduction to independence, not her introduction to sexual violence. Twenty-six years ago, the U.S. Department of Justice warned that between one-fifth and one-quarter of college women could be expected to experience completed or attempted rape during their college careers. Parents worry about tuition, roommates, grades, and whether their daughters are eating properly. Perhaps we should spend more time asking whether the universities collecting those tuition checks are doing their jobs. Indiana University wasn't unique. In 2000, student Jill Behrman disappeared while bicycling. Her remains were discovered years later. In 2011, Lauren Spierer disappeared after a night out in Bloomington. Her disappearance remains unsolved. Lauren's parents have spent fifteen years without an answer to the most basic question imaginable: Where is our daughter? At the University of North Carolina Wilmington, two young women were murdered just 30 days apart in 2004. Related: Don't Look Down: America's Democracy Is Under Strain—and the World Is Watching On May 5, Jessica Faulkner was raped and murdered in her dormitory by fellow student Curtis Dixon, who had a history of stalking and threatening women at other universities. That history had not been disclosed on his application to UNCW. I spoke with Jessica's father, John Faulkner. It was a painful conversation on many levels, one I have never forgotten. John subsequently advocated for stronger criminal-background screening at North Carolina universities, hoping to prevent another family from experiencing what his had endured. You might think Jessica's murder would have put an entire university on heightened alert. But just weeks later, Christen Naujoks and her mother sought help from campus police because Christen was being stalked and threatened by a former boyfriend. According to her mother's account, when they requested a different parking space for Christen's protection, they were reportedly told that changing hers would mean changing everyone's. This was the same university where a young woman had just been murdered. Christen obtained a protective order. It didn't save her. On June 4, 2004, she was shot to death outside her apartment. Two young women. One university. Thirty days. I haven't forgotten Jessica Faulkner or Christen Naujoks, and I never will. [PHOTOGRAPHS TO INSERT: Jessica Faulkner and Christen Naujoks, side by side] At Notre Dame, Lizzy Seeberg reported a sexual assault involving a football player in 2010. She faced intimidating messages afterward and died by suicide days later. At the University of Virginia, Yeardley Love was murdered by her former boyfriend in 2010. At the University of Utah, Lauren McCluskey was murdered in 2018 after repeatedly seeking help concerning threats from a former boyfriend. More than twenty years have passed since Jessica and Christen were murdered. Yet the systemic indifference their cases exposed remains disturbingly familiar in the handling of sexual violence allegations at Cornell University today. He Said. He Said. For years, police and prosecutors explained to me why sexual assault cases couldn't move forward. He said. She said. I eventually wrote an article called He Said. He Said. because that familiar expression doesn't accurately describe what happens. The accused says the encounter was consensual. And too often, that's where the investigation begins and ends. There is no meaningful she said. Whatever she says seems to carry little weight against his assertion of consent. At Cornell University, a young woman has alleged that she was gang raped by fraternity members who, according to her account, used social media to invite other men to join them while the assault was taking place. How morally depraved would you have to be to participate in something like that? According to reporting on the case, the prosecutor declined criminal charges without personally interviewing the complainant or reviewing her complete interview transcript. Apparently, hearing from the woman herself wasn't considered essential. And we're still calling this He Said. She Said. Related: He said. He said. End of Story. A New Generation, the Same Old Misogyny What troubles me about the Cornell allegations goes beyond the alleged assault itself. It's the suggestion that violence against a woman could become a spectacle, something to share, even an invitation for others to participate. What kind of culture produces that attitude toward women? Perhaps we shouldn't be surprised when men like Andrew and Tristan Tate cultivate enormous audiences while promoting deeply troubling attitudes toward women. Both face serious criminal charges in the United Kingdom involving alleged sexual violence and trafficking. They deny wrongdoing and are entitled to the presumption of innocence. But their criminal cases are only part of the story. What troubles me is the audience for a brand of masculinity that treats domination as strength and women as something to be controlled. We spent generations telling our daughters they deserved equality. Who is telling our sons that equality isn't an insult? Today we have domestic violence laws, sexual assault statutes, Title IX, the Clery Act, and enough university policies to wallpaper a football stadium. We've made progress in legislation. I'm considerably less impressed with our progress in accountability. Justice Delayed Is Justice Denied And what happens when women turn to the agencies charged with holding these institutions accountable? Apparently, they wait. And wait. At Lehigh University, where nineteen-year-old Jeanne Clery was raped and murdered in her residence hall in 1986, a federal complaint has reportedly remained unresolved for six years. It was Jeanne's murder that led her parents to fight for the federal campus crime reporting law that bears her name. Even at the university where that tragedy occurred, the system established in its aftermath appears unable to deliver timely accountability. At George Mason University, a woman who had survived sexual violence had neither the strength nor the emotional reserves to pursue a complaint against the man she accused. But when she learned that the man she identified as her assailant, who had a serious criminal history, had obtained a teaching position, she found the courage to come forward. Not for herself, but because she feared for the young women who might find themselves in his classroom. Nearly four years later, according to her account, her federal Clery Act complaint remains unresolved. She says she has received neither meaningful protection nor justice, while the man she accused has gone on to pursue a law degree. She came forward to protect others. Who has protected her? We created a system to police the institutions that failed to protect these women. But who is policing that system? Of All Places, Safety Harbor The failure to protect women isn't confined to university campuses. It follows them into their homes, their relationships, and sometimes to their graves. On October 13, 2026, in a Florida town called Safety Harbor, 30-year-old Jessica Antolini was shot in the face and then run over by a vehicle, allegedly driven by her assailant. Her boyfriend, Christopher “Dodge” Smith, has been charged with first-degree murder and child abuse. He is presumed innocent unless convicted. Jessica died two days later. Smith's five-year-old daughter and their dog were in the vehicle when police located it. I cannot stop thinking about that little girl and what she may have seen or heard that night. Five years old. What kind of memories will she carry into adulthood? And of all places, Safety Harbor. Women can report abuse, seek restraining orders, file complaints, and invoke federal protections. But those protections mean little when the people responsible for enforcing them fail to act. Jessica Antolini is dead. And countless women are still waiting for somebody to take their complaints seriously. I still remember that billboard on Interstate 65. HELL IS REAL. For the women who have endured violence, the families who have buried daughters, and the children left behind, it isn't a theological argument. It's something they've lived. October will end, as it always does. But we should remember what this month represents, not just during October, but during the other eleven months of the year. It's been twenty years since my daughter was raped. We've made progress, but nowhere near enough, and nowhere near fast enough. I can only hope that twenty years from now, no one will still have reason to write this same article.
